KIPLMC/Geometry.lean.title: The scaled particle potential and its gradient
KIPLMC/Geometry.lean.summary:
The shared IPLA state stores \(z=(\theta,X^1/\sqrt N,\ldots,X^N/\sqrt N)\) in a Euclidean coordinate space with independent parameter and latent dimensions. This section keeps physical time, scaling velocities by the same spatial map. In this convention the kinetic temperature is \(1/N\), the potential is the particle average \(\bar U_N\), and the force is its gradient. It is equivalent to the manuscript's additional time change but uses the same kinetic step.

The scaled average potential keeps curvature and smoothness independent of particle count in physical time. Its coordinate derivatives explain why the parameter force is averaged while physical latent forces are unaveraged.

steps.title: The averaged potential and its gradient
steps.body:
The scaled particle state space is the scaled Euclidean IPLA state. The existing lifted potential is \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\). Define \(\bar U_N=V_N/N\) and \(F=\nabla V_N/N\). To prove \(\nabla\bar U_N=F\), compare their inner products against an arbitrary vector. The derivative rule for a scalar multiple gives \(D\bar U_N[w]=N^{-1}DV_N[w]\), and the inner-product characterization of gradients identifies the two vectors. The argument uses equality of all inner products, the proved differentiability of the lifted potential, and the derivative rule for a constant multiple. For \(N>0\), cancellation of the nonzero particle number gives \(V_N=N\bar U_N\).

The spatial scaling places the common parameter and all latent particles in one Euclidean space while preserving the physical latent coordinates through multiplication by \(\sqrt N\). Dividing the lifted potential by \(N\) makes its gradient the physical-time force. The potential and temperature must be scaled consistently.

steps.title: Average the lifted strong convexity
steps.body:
The existing particle geometry proves \(V_N\) is \(Nm\)-strongly convex whenever the pair potential is \(m\)-strongly convex. Multiply its convex-combination inequality by \(N^{-1}>0\): the function terms become \(\bar U_N\), and the quadratic correction \(N^{-1}(Nm)\|x-y\|^2/2\) becomes \(m\|x-y\|^2/2\). The argument writes the strong-convexity inequality, obtains the lifted inequality, multiplies it by the nonnegative inverse particle number, and uses cancellation of nonzero denominators and expansion of the scalar polynomials to cancel constants. The proof requires positive particle count but imposes no artificial equality of the parameter and latent dimensions.

The quadratic correction in strong convexity scales by exactly the same scalar as the potential. Since the lifted potential’s curvature is \(Nm\), averaging removes the particle factor. The resulting force geometry therefore has the original pair curvature, regardless of the total particle-space dimension.

steps.title: The mean parameter force and unaveraged latent force
steps.body:
The parameter block of \( abla V_N\) is the sum of pair parameter gradients, so \(F_ heta=N^{-1}\sum_i abla_ heta U( heta,X^i)\). Each latent block of \( abla V_N\) is \(\sqrt N abla_xU\). Dividing by \(N\) and undoing the spatial scaling gives \(\sqrt N F_i= abla_xU( heta,X^i)\). The parameter proof simplifies with the existing gradient-coordinate theorem. The latent proof expands coordinate scalar multiplication, groups the coefficient into \((\sqrt N)^2N^{-1}\), rewrites \((\sqrt N)^2=N\), and cancels the nonzero \(N\). These identities verify the force used by both particle algorithms.

The parameter appears in every summand, so its derivative is a particle average. Each latent coordinate appears in just one summand, and undoing the coordinate scaling recovers its unaveraged derivative. These different factors explain the apparent asymmetry between parameter and latent equations.

steps.title: The force retains the pair smoothness constant
steps.body:
The shared lifted gradient has Lipschitz constant \(NL\). Since \(F=\nabla V_N/N\), its difference satisfies \(\|F(x)-F(y)\|\le N^{-1}(NL)\|x-y\|=L\|x-y\|\). The argument starts from the existing lifted Lipschitz estimate, rewrites norms of scalar multiples with the nonnegative inverse particle count, multiplies the inequality by that inverse, and cancels \(N\). This proves that the physical-time scaled force has a smoothness constant independent of the number of particles, as required for the particle-independent deterministic contraction rate.

The average-potential normalization cancels the lifted gradient’s factor \(N\). Consequently neither the strong-convexity nor smoothness constant grows with particle count in physical time. The dimension still affects thermal moments, but the deterministic contraction rate is particle independent.

KIPLMC/Exponential.lean.title: The KIPLMC1 exponential update in parameter and latent coordinates
KIPLMC/Exponential.lean.summary:
The particle exponential step is the exponential update with the average-potential gradient. KIPLMC1 supplies the proved averaged particle force and the common scaled-coordinate thermal amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). The coordinate identities recover the paper's Algorithm 1 directly, including its separate velocity and position innovations. Noise covariance and independent-Gaussian law conditions must still be established for any stochastic convergence theorem.

The particle method uses the common exponential response with thermal covariance scaled by the inverse particle count. Exact coordinate identities recover the parameter and latent updates while preserving correlated position–velocity noise.

steps.title: The exponential update at particle temperature
steps.body:
The kinetic noise amplitude is \(a_N=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). The KIPLMC1 update is the exponential map with force \(F\) and additive phase innovation \(a_N\,\text{noise}\). Consequently every block uses exactly the same friction response functions. In physical time and scaled coordinates this is an inverse temperature \(N\) kinetic system. The definition accepts arbitrary innovations; when used as the algorithm their velocity–position pair must have the common Gram covariance from the kinetic library.

In scaled coordinates the equilibrium velocity covariance is \(I/N\). The fluctuation–dissipation amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) corresponds to that temperature. The response covariance itself is the common exponential Gram matrix; the amplitude is applied afterward to the entire correlated pair.

steps.title: Recover both parameter updates
steps.body:
Parameter coordinates are unchanged by spatial rescaling. Substitute \(F_ heta=N^{-1}\sum_i abla_ heta U_i\) in the two shared expressions:

\[V^{ heta+}=\psi_0V^ heta- rac{\psi_1}N\sum_i abla_ heta U_i+a_N\xi_ heta,\quad heta^+= heta+\psi_1V^ heta- rac{\psi_2}N\sum_i abla_ heta U_i+a_N\xi'_ heta.\]

The proofs unfold the shared map, evaluate scalar multiplication in Euclidean coordinates, rewrite the proved force identity, and normalize division as multiplication by an inverse. The distinct projections of the innovation pair retain the correlated but generally unequal velocity and position increments.

The parameter position receives an integrated version of the same velocity noise. Thus the two displayed innovations are correlated even though they are written in different equations. Keeping their common block law is necessary for the algorithm’s correct transition measure.

steps.title: Undo the latent temperature and force scaling
steps.body:
For \(N>0\), \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The proof combines square roots using nonnegativity of \(N\), then cancels the positive particle number inside the root. Multiply each latent coordinate of the shared step by \(\sqrt N\). The force identity gives \(\sqrt NF_i=\nabla_xU_i\); the amplitude identity restores \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) noise. Thus the physical latent velocity and position updates have the unaveraged pair force and the paper's latent thermal scale. The two coordinate proofs distribute multiplication, rewrite these exact identities and finish scalar rearrangement with expansion of the scalar polynomials.

The spatial factor \(\sqrt N\) simultaneously restores the unaveraged latent force and the unit-temperature latent noise. This explains why physical latent updates have familiar single-particle coefficients while the parameter noise remains reduced by particle averaging.

steps.title: The numerical recursion from a supplied innovation stream
steps.body:
The KIPLMC1 sequence starts from the given phase and uses innovation number \(n\) in the successor update. Each step is the shared exponential map specialized to the particle force. Recursive construction proves there is an explicit sequence for every prescribed stream; it is not an assumed sequence satisfying a desired estimate. To obtain the paper's random chain, one must additionally equip this stream with independent centered Gaussian pairs of the right covariance and prove its independence from initialization, measurability and finite moments.

Once an initial phase and the full innovation stream are supplied, the recursion determines every state. If that stream has the independent correlated-Gaussian block law and is independent of initialization, pushing the inputs through the recursion gives the Gaussian Markov sampler.

KIPLMC/Splitting.lean.title: The KIPLMC2 thermostat–kick–drift–kick–thermostat update
KIPLMC/Splitting.lean.summary:
In scaled physical-time particle coordinates every velocity block has temperature \(1/N\). The parameter coordinates stay unchanged. Multiplying a latent coordinate by \(\sqrt N\) recovers the physical latent position and velocity and the unit-temperature latent noise used in Algorithm 2. The module proves these coordinate identities for the five-subflow map; no OBABO contraction theorem is hidden in the definitions.

The particle OBABO map retains the exact order of the five substeps in scaled coordinates. Undoing latent scaling restores the physical thermostat temperature and the original pair-gradient half kicks.

steps.title: The scaled thermostat and half velocity
steps.body:
Let \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and \(\sigma_N=\sqrt{(1-\delta^2)/N}\). The thermostat amplitude is \(\sigma_N\), and the KIPLMC2 update uses it with the force \(F\) to the shared OBABO map, and the half-step velocity records \(v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma_N\xi-hF(x)/2\). The algorithm uses this newly formed half velocity for its full position drift. The second force kick is evaluated at the new position, and the final OU half step receives the distinct noise \(\xi'\). The position and velocity formulas follow by evaluating these five successive maps.

The first thermostat refresh and first force kick create the velocity used by the drift. The final force is evaluated at the newly updated position before the second thermostat refresh. Reordering either evaluation would produce a different splitting method.

steps.title: The parameter half velocity contains the average gradient
steps.body:
Evaluating the half velocity on parameter index \(j\) gives

\[(v_{1/2})_{\theta,j}=\delta v_{\theta,j}+\sigma_N\xi_{\theta,j} -\frac{h}{2N}\sum_i\nabla_\theta U(\theta,X^i)_j.\]

The proof unfolds the half-velocity definition, distributes coordinate evaluation over vector addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, then substitutes the parameter-average force identity. The remaining equality is scalar rational algebra, verified by distributing scalar products. This proof keeps the particle mean in the force rather than adding an assumed algorithm-equivalence premise.

The average parameter gradient is inherited from the averaged potential. It is multiplied by the half-step length because this is one of the two B stages. The full parameter force action over a step is distributed between the old and new positions.

steps.title: Undo latent scaling in the first O and B substeps
steps.body:
The thermostat identity is \(\sqrt N\sigma_N=\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\). Its proof combines square roots and cancels the positive \(N\) inside the argument. Multiplying the latent half velocity by \(\sqrt N\) then gives

\[\sqrt N(v_{1/2})_i=\delta(\sqrt Nv_i)+\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\xi_i-\frac h2\nabla_xU(\theta,X^i).\]

The coordinate proof expands multiplication through the three terms, applies the proved thermostat and force-unscaling identities, and normalizes multiplication order with expansion of the scalar polynomials. This yields exactly the physical latent OU refresh and unaveraged force kick.

The latent scaling cancels the temperature reduction in thermostat amplitude. Its physical noise is therefore the standard unit-temperature OU noise. The same scaling cancels the averaging in the latent force, giving the physical pair-gradient kick.

steps.title: Recover physical parameter and latent position drifts
steps.body:
The common position formula is \(z^+=z+h v_{1/2}\). Its parameter coordinate reads \(\theta^+=\theta+hV^\theta_{1/2}\) directly because that coordinate was not scaled; its theorem is definitional. In a latent coordinate, multiply both sides by \(\sqrt N\) and distribute: \(X^{i+}=X^i+hV^{x_i}_{1/2}\). The argument rewrites the shared position identity, simplifies Euclidean coordinate operations and proves the scalar distributive equality with expansion of the scalar polynomials. Together with the half-velocity and final-velocity identities, these are the paper's complete pointwise OBABO stages. Gaussian transition laws and their numerical bias remain separate analytic assertions.

Position does not receive an independent direct noise in this splitting. Its randomness is transported by the refreshed half velocity. The parameter and latent position formulas therefore follow from the same deterministic drift stage after their respective coordinate scalings.

KIPLMC/Target.lean.title: The particle Gibbs phase measure and sharp parameter concentration
KIPLMC/Target.lean.summary:
The velocity-first phase target is the product of an explicit Gaussian thermal velocity measure and the already normalized lifted Gibbs position measure. Its parameter marginal is the powered likelihood, and its concentration radius has the paper's sharp dimension coefficient. These results concern the defined probability measure; the section deliberately does not claim invariance of that measure under a kinetic diffusion.

The phase target combines explicit thermal Gaussian velocities with the normalized lifted Gibbs position law. Its powered-likelihood parameter marginal supplies the sharp equilibrium concentration around the unique marginal maximizer.

steps.title: Construct thermal velocities as a Gaussian pushforward
steps.body:
Start with the standard Gaussian on the scaled particle Euclidean space and map \(v\mapsto v/\sqrt N\). The resulting thermal Gaussian measure has covariance \(I/N\) for positive \(N\). The probability proof uses measurability of the scalar map, evaluates its preimage of the whole space, and obtains mass one. The definition also makes sense at \(N=0\) under the convention \(0^{-1}=0\), but the physical target and subsequent normalization theorems require \(N>0\). No unspecified Gaussian velocity law is assumed.

The velocity pushforward is a centered Gaussian with covariance \(I/N\) for positive particle count. Its finite moments follow from Gaussian scaling. This gives both the exact thermal initialization and the equilibrium velocity factor used in the particle coupling proof.

steps.title: Normalize the product and compute its position marginal
steps.body:
The kinetic Gibbs target is \(\mathcal N(0,I/N)\otimes\pi_N\), with velocity first. Joint strong convexity and differentiability of the original pair potential imply that the shared lifted Gibbs target \(\pi_N\) is a probability measure. Both factors have total mass one, so their product does as well. Mapping the product by its second projection integrates out the first factor, whose total mass is one, so the result is exactly \(\pi_N\). The proof uses the second marginal of a product measure and simplifies the mass scalar. This computes the normalized marginal rather than merely comparing unnormalized density expressions.

The position density is proportional to \(e^{-V_N}\), while the kinetic velocity density is proportional to \(e^{-N\|v\|^2/2}\). Their product is the physical-temperature phase target. Product normalization immediately gives its independence structure and exact position marginal.

steps.title: The powered likelihood parameter marginal
steps.body:
Map the phase target to \(\theta\) by composing position projection with the parameter continuous linear map. The pushforward composition theorem identifies this with first taking the position marginal and then the parameter marginal. The preceding result gives the exact lifted Gibbs position law; the shared IPLA theorem identifies its parameter marginal as \(p_\theta(y)^N\) after normalization. Measurability of both maps is provided explicitly. The theorem therefore connects the phase target with the same normalized marginal target used by the concentration proof.

Integrating latent particles factorizes conditionally on the common parameter: each contributes the same marginal likelihood factor. Their product is the \(N\)-th power of that likelihood. The normalized pushforward identity makes this statistical interpretation precise.

steps.title: The unique marginal maximizer and its sharp second moment
steps.body:
Joint strong convexity makes the negative log marginal strongly convex after latent integration. The shared IPLA theorem supplies existence and uniqueness of its minimizer, equivalently of the marginal likelihood maximizer. For that \(\theta_*\), the sharp concentration theorem gives \(\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\pi_\Theta\le d_\theta/(Nm)\). These results concern the normalized powered-likelihood marginal obtained above. The last theorem expresses the square-root bound in the existing extended-nonnegative transport notation as \(\left(\int\|P_\theta z-\theta_*\|^2\,d\pi_N(z)\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\).

The parameter concentration scale is \(N^{-1/2}\), with the sharp dimension coefficient \(\sqrt{d_\theta/m}\). It describes equilibrium error relative to the likelihood maximizer. Numerical discretization and finite-time initialization errors must be added separately in an algorithmic bound.

KIPLMC/Dynamics.lean.title: Physical-time particle integral solutions and synchronous contraction
KIPLMC/Dynamics.lean.summary:
The particle-average potential has the original pair curvature and smoothness constants, so the physical-time kinetic system can reuse the shared existence and nonlinear contraction theorems directly. The temperature changes the additive noise amplitude; the synchronous contraction does not depend on that amplitude because the common forcing cancels. The results here are explicit path statements, not stationarity statements.

The average force meets the shared kinetic existence and contraction hypotheses. Common-input cancellation explains why physical-time deterministic contraction does not deteriorate with particle number or total state dimension.

steps.title: Verify differentiability and smoothness of the average
steps.body:
The lifted potential is differentiable whenever the pair potential is differentiable. Multiplying its value by the constant \(1/N\) preserves differentiability, yielding differentiability of the average potential. The gradient has already been identified pointwise with the particle force. Equality at every position identifies the two vector fields. The average-gradient smoothness bound therefore gives the same Lipschitz estimate for the particle force. The result uses the original pair constant \(L\), independent of \(N\).

The gradient identity is essential for applying a potential-based contraction theorem: it ensures the defined force is the derivative of the stated average potential. Smoothness is then inherited with the original pair constant, while strong convexity is inherited by averaging the lifted inequality.

steps.title: Apply the kinetic integral-equation construction to the real particle force
steps.body:
With \(N>0\), the force is globally Lipschitz. The shared kinetic existence theorem therefore constructs a continuous phase path satisfying \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tD_F(Y_s)ds+(B_t,0)\) on any finite nonnegative horizon, for every continuous velocity forcing starting at zero. The integral equation uses inverse mass one because the force already equals \(\nabla\bar U_N\). Choosing physical-time Brownian amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) gives the intended scaled particle forcing, but a complete probabilistic strong-solution result also identifies the driving Brownian law and independence conditions.

The forcing is any continuous velocity input in the deterministic existence statement. The specified Brownian choice supplies the desired thermal process afterward. This separates solving the integral equation from identifying the probability law of its driving source.

steps.title: The nonlinear contraction rate is independent of particle dimension
steps.body:
Apply the shared potential contraction theorem to \(\bar U_N\). Its required hypotheses are derived by the average-potential differentiability, strong-convexity and smoothness theorems. Rewrite each gradient in the difference equation using \(\nabla\bar U_N=F\). With equal initial velocities, \(\gamma>0\), and \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\), the resulting bound is \(\|x_t-y_t\|\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\|x_0-y_0\|\). Neither \(N\) nor \(d_\theta+Nd_x\) appears in its rate. The theorem still explicitly requires continuous paths satisfying the noise-cancelled derivative equations; it does not replace construction of a stationary kinetic reference or taking the Wasserstein infimum.

The common additive noise cancels even though its amplitude depends on particle count. The remaining difference equation sees only the average-potential geometry. The dimension and temperature therefore affect equilibrium and discretization moments, while leaving the synchronous physical-time rate unchanged.

KIPLMC/Laws.lean.title: Measurable particle transitions and the laws of their recursions
KIPLMC/Laws.lean.summary:
The pathwise algorithm maps become probability transitions by integrating them against independent fresh-noise measures. This section reuses the generic Markov-law construction and independence argument already proved for ULA. For KIPLMC1 it accepts a specified correlated phase innovation law; KIPLMC2 uses an explicit pair of independent standard Gaussian vectors for its two OU half steps. Law equality is kept distinct from convergence rates.

Both explicit particle recursions are identified with their independent-noise Markov iterates. The exponential transition retains correlated response pairs, while OBABO retains two distinct independent thermostat noises.

steps.title: The OBABO noise law and measurability of both step maps
steps.body:
The thermostat noise law is the product of two standard Gaussian measures on the particle Euclidean space. Its product probability property gives total mass one. Lipschitzness of the particle force implies continuity. Unfolding the exponential or OBABO map shows that each is built from this continuous force, coordinate projections, addition and scalar multiplication, so each uncurried state–noise map is continuous and hence measurable. The argument supplies force continuity first, applies measurability of continuous maps, and uses continuity of each operation in the finite composition.

The two thermostat noises form an independent product of Gaussian vector measures. Continuity of the force makes each finite-stage update measurable. Both particle algorithms therefore define probability transitions by pushing forward the state/noise product.

steps.title: Define numerical laws by independent-noise pushforwards
steps.body:
The KIPLMC1 law sequence applies the shared Markov recursion with the exponential step, an initial phase measure \(\mu\), and a supplied innovation measure \(\eta\). The KIPLMC2 law sequence uses the OBABO step and its fixed two-Gaussian noise measure. Each successor law is the pushforward of the product of the current-state law and the fresh-noise law. The probability theorems invoke the proved step measurability and probability of the initial and innovation measures, so every iterate is a probability measure. For KIPLMC1 the covariance specification of \(\eta\) remains explicit and separate; probability alone does not identify the intended correlated Gaussian law.

At each step take a fresh innovation independent of the present state and apply the specified map. Integrating this update against its innovation measure defines one transition. Repeated pushforward gives the numerical laws without assuming an underlying chain with the desired estimates.

steps.title: The explicit exponential recursion has the Markov law
steps.body:
First show that the KIPLMC1 sequence equals the generic noise-driven recursion. Induction is exact: both start at the same phase and their successor expressions use the same step and innovation number. The law theorem then assumes a measurable initial random phase, a jointly independent innovation sequence with common law \(\eta\), and independence of initialization from the whole sequence. The shared generic result derives the law at every step; no additional per-step state–noise independence premise is inserted. Rewriting the explicit recursion by the proved equality yields the pushforward identity with the KIPLMC1 laws. This theorem establishes equality of the recursion law and the iterated transition law, while a quantitative sampling estimate still requires moment and coupling analysis for the specified Gaussian innovation.

The explicit recursion is a measurable function of initialization and the innovation prefix. Independence of the next block gives the one-step transition identity. Induction then identifies its law with the iterated exponential transition measure.

steps.title: The independent-Gaussian OBABO trajectory has the constructed transition law
steps.body:
The KIPLMC2 sequence iterates the OBABO map with the two thermostat vectors from each supplied noise pair. If these pairs are independent across time, have the product law of two independent standard Gaussian vectors, and are independent of initialization, then the pushforward of the pathwise recursion equals the KIPLMC2 laws at every step. The generic independence theorem derives independence of the current state from the fresh pair from these global assumptions. The proof is a direct reuse of that theorem with the established measurable OBABO map. Independence within each pair is given by its product Gaussian law; it is not confused with the independent sequence of pairs. This completes the algorithm-law correspondence, while contraction and the discrete invariant-measure bias remain separate quantitative conclusions.

The same argument applies to the two-thermostat recursion, keeping the two noises distinct and independent. Their common block law is used at every step. Thus the trajectory’s pushforward agrees with the constructed OBABO Markov law.

steps.title: Choose the constructed kinetic Gaussian for Algorithm 1
steps.body:
The generic law identity accepts a specified iid innovation measure. The Gaussian KIPLMC1 law sequence uses the correlated Gaussian measure constructed in the explicit correlated particle-noise construction, whose spatial pairs have the shared kinetic Gram covariance. Thus the transition and its particle scaling are explicit. The earlier iid realization theorem specializes to this measure, with ordinary independence of initialization and fresh innovations. A convergence theorem must still derive a target comparison for these laws; the definition does not assert such a bound.

For Algorithm 1 the innovation law is the constructed exponential response Gaussian, including its off-diagonal covariance. Substituting that law specializes the generic transition to the correlated-Gaussian sampler. Independent velocity and position noises would define a different law.

KIPLMC/Rescaling.lean.title: Velocity and time rescaling of the exponential update
KIPLMC/Rescaling.lean.summary:
The physical-time particle realization can be expressed in unit-temperature kinetic coordinates by scaling velocity and the clock. This section proves the deterministic conjugacy of the exponential map and the damping identity. Gaussian covariance scaling and Brownian time-change laws remain distinct probabilistic results.

The deterministic velocity-and-clock conjugacy converts the physical average force to the unit-temperature sum-potential force. Position is fixed, while response and damping identities control the remaining phase coefficients.

steps.title: Invert the velocity scale
steps.body:
The velocity rescaling sends \((v,x)\) to \((cv,x)\). If \(c\ne0\), applying the inverse scale yields \((c^{-1}cv,x)=(v,x)\). The argument simplifies the nested scalar action and cancels the nonzero factor. Position is unchanged, so a parameter-position projection commutes with this part of the change of variables.

The velocity-only map is invertible for a nonzero scale and fixes every position observable. Hence it changes the phase coordinates without changing the parameter sample itself. Later law identities exploit exactly this unchanged position projection.

steps.title: Conjugate the shared exponential step
steps.body:
The exact coefficient scaling gives \(\psi_{c\gamma,k}(h/c)=\psi_{\gamma,k}(h)/c^k\). Apply a step with force \(g\), friction \(c\gamma\), duration \(h/c\), initial velocity \(cv\), and additive innovation whose velocity component is also scaled by \(c\). Its result equals the velocity rescaling of a physical-time step with force \(g/c^2\), friction \(\gamma\), duration \(h\). One proves the two scalar cancellations for the first primitive, expands the map coordinatewise, rewrites all coefficient scales, and normalizes the resulting vector identities with vector-space algebra. The innovation here is already additive; obtaining its prescribed Gaussian law under this conjugacy requires a separate covariance computation.

The response with one time primitive acquires one inverse clock factor; the position-force response acquires two. Combining those factors with the scaled velocity and force gives the deterministic step conjugacy. The noise law must be transformed separately because its two response coordinates scale differently.

steps.title: The invariant friction–step product and particle scale
steps.body:
The OU damping depends on the product \(\gamma h\), so \(e^{-(c\gamma)(h/c)/2}=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) for \(c\ne0\). The proof unfolds the damping definition, reduces equality of exponentials to equality of exponents, and cancels the nonzero factor with cancellation of nonzero denominators. For the particle choice \(c=\sqrt N\), the coefficient identity \(((\sqrt N)^2)^{-1}=N^{-1}\) follows from the nonnegative square-root square theorem. Consequently the sum-potential force in rescaled time corresponds to the average-potential force in physical time.

Thermostat damping depends only on the dimensionless product of friction and step, so that product is invariant under the clock change. Choosing the scale \(\sqrt N\) converts the average force into the sum-potential force and simultaneously normalizes thermal velocity.

KIPLMC/Noise.lean.title: Correlated Gaussian velocity and position innovations in particle coordinates
KIPLMC/Noise.lean.summary:
Velocity and position innovations within a coordinate share a Brownian source and are correlated. Distinct spatial coordinates are independent. This section constructs that joint probability measure using the kinetic library's two-dimensional Gram Gaussian, directly on the parameter-and-particle coordinate set. It works also when one of the dimensions is zero.

The innovation is built from independent spatial response blocks. Packing preserves each block’s correlation and gives the finite-dimensional Gaussian vectors used by the defined first particle algorithm.

steps.title: Construct independent spatial Gaussian blocks and assemble phase vectors
steps.body:
The coordinate set is \(I=\{1,\ldots,d_\theta\}\sqcup(\{1,\ldots,N\}\times\{1,\ldots,d_x\})\). For each \(i\in I\), take the shared kinetic Gaussian \((\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_i\prime)\sim\mathcal N(0,C_{\gamma,h})\), independently across \(i\). Their finite product measure is the independent spatial Gaussian blocks. The assembly map collects the first entries into the velocity vector and the second entries into the position vector. The proof defines these two Euclidean vectors with the Euclidean identification and proves the map measurable coordinate by coordinate. Pushing the product measure forward gives the correlated exponential noise. Probability follows from the Gaussian probability properties and preservation of total mass under the measurable map; no normalization assumption is supplied.

For each scaled particle-space coordinate, draw one two-response Gaussian block. Independent products over coordinates preserve the within-block velocity–position covariance. Packing all first responses and all second responses produces the two vector innovations used in the update.

steps.title: Coordinate independence and within-pair covariance
steps.body:
The product-space evaluation maps are independent, so the Gaussian blocks belonging to distinct coordinates are independent. Evaluating the assembled velocity and position at a fixed spatial coordinate recovers its original two-dimensional Gaussian block exactly. The proof composes the two pushforwards, proves equality of the composed function with the block evaluation map by checking the two possible indices, and uses the product-measure evaluation law. The covariance of the pair is therefore exactly the kinetic Gram matrix, already proved positive semidefinite in the shared library. Multiplication by \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) is performed by the particle step, not by this base noise law.

Different spatial coordinate blocks are independent because they are projections of different product factors. The two entries of a single block generally remain correlated through their common response Gram matrix. Both properties are required to recover the intended particle transition law.

KIPLMC/FlowLaw.lean.title: Wasserstein contraction of the physical-time particle position laws
KIPLMC/FlowLaw.lean.summary:
The scaled configuration space is \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+Nd_x}\), with potential \(\bar U_N=V_N/N\). Its gradient is the physical-time particle force. The original pair potential's strong convexity and gradient Lipschitz constants pass to \(\bar U_N\) unchanged. Consequently the shared kinetic flow theorem applies with the original \(m,L,\gamma\), independently of the number of particles. This section constructs a probability law by an independent product and pushforward, and proves contraction of those laws. It does not assume Gibbs stationarity or identify an arbitrary forcing law with Brownian motion.

The physical-time integral solution defines a measurable position endpoint map. Extending every initial plan by a common independent source gives the Wasserstein contraction of its output laws.

steps.title: Use the Borel structure of continuous forcing paths
steps.body:

The shared OBABO position bias is \(6\sqrt2\gamma\prime h\prime\sqrt{d_z}(4\sqrt{L\prime}+L\prime h\prime/2)/m\prime\). Substitute the exact clock and curvature values. Since \(\sqrt{c^2L}=c\sqrt L\), cancellation gives

\[\frac{6\sqrt2\gamma}{m}h\sqrt{\frac{d_z}{N}}\left(4\sqrt L+\frac{Lh}{2}\right),\qquad d_z=d_\theta+Nd_x.\]

The algebraic theorem records the exact equality of the two expressions, not just an asymptotic comparison.

After substitution, the only dimensional fluctuation factor is the physical thermal radius \(\sqrt{d_z/N}\). Its square is the latent dimension plus the parameter dimension divided by the particle count. The remaining friction, smoothness, and step factors are exactly those of the shared OBABO local-error accumulation.

steps.title: Apply the OBABO sampling theorem
steps.body:
The sum potential inherits strong convexity \(Nm\) and smoothness \(NL\) from the original joint potential. Its Gibbs target is exactly the defined lifted particle target. The theorem applies the proved unit-temperature sampler bound, transports its position law through the exact conjugacy, and simplifies the rate and bias. It proves both finiteness of the output Wasserstein distance and

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi_N)\le\sqrt2\left(1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma}\right)^{n/2}W_2(\nu,\pi_N)+\frac{6\sqrt2\gamma}{m}h\sqrt{\frac{d_z}{N}}\left(4\sqrt L+\frac{Lh}{2}\right).\]

The two-thermostat Gaussian laws are part of the constructed Markov recursion. No stationarity, reference-path or local-error estimate is assumed.

The numerical law, target, and all analytic assumptions have been identified before invoking the shared result. Its finite-output transport conclusion therefore transfers along with its inequality. The resulting physical-time bound applies to the two-thermostat Gaussian particle recursion.

steps.title: Project to the parameter and add the sharp concentration term
steps.body:
The initial finite second moment and strong convexity give a finite initial transport distance. The preceding theorem gives finite output transport. The parameter projection has norm at most one, so its RMS error around the unique MMLE is bounded by the position transport distance plus the Gibbs parameter RMS error. The latter is at most \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\). The final theorem therefore adds this third term to the KIPLMC2 sampling estimate and expresses the result as the square root of the parameter-error integral.

Project an output coupling to the common parameter and use its nonexpansiveness. The equilibrium powered marginal lies within the sharp statistical radius of the unique maximizer. Adding this radius to the numerical transport bound yields the displayed parameter RMS estimate.

KIPLMC/OBABOPaperRate.lean.title: The printed KIPLMC2 bound with an explicit uniform constant
KIPLMC/OBABOPaperRate.lean.summary:
The preceding sampler theorem gives a smaller thermal discretization term. This section derives the precise coarser form printed in the supplied manuscript, including its additional transient term. The implicit constant is replaced by an explicit expression that depends only on \(m,L,\gamma\), and the final result concerns the parameter-error integral.

The sharper proved physical bound implies the manuscript’s coarser upper bound term by term. An explicit constant reveals its dependence on curvature and friction while remaining uniform in particle count and dimension.

steps.title: Comparison of the square-root geometric factor with the stated exponential bound
steps.body:
Let \(r=\sqrt{1-mh/(3\gamma)}\). The scalar bound \(1-x\le e^{-x}\), followed by taking square roots, gives \(r\le e^{-mh/(6\gamma)}\). Raising to the integer iteration index proves \(r^n\le e^{-mhn/(6\gamma)}\). The proof also handles a nonpositive square-root argument directly, so the scalar upper bound itself does not need an extra admissibility hypothesis.

The square-root geometric factor is converted to an exponential with half its linear exponent. This gives the manuscript’s exponential decay in iteration count. Raising the scalar bound to an integer power preserves it because both sides are nonnegative.

steps.title: An explicit uniform constant
steps.body:
The allowed step satisfies \(h\le m/(33\gamma^3)\). Consequently the physical bias coefficient is bounded by

\[B=\frac{6\sqrt2\gamma}{m}\left(4\sqrt L+\frac{Lm}{66\gamma^3}\right).\]

Choose \(C=\sqrt2+B+1/\sqrt m\). All three summands are nonnegative, so \(C\) dominates the transient coefficient, bias coefficient and equilibrium concentration coefficient separately. One proves these comparisons from positivity, without permitting dependence on the particle count, dimensions or step.

The step-dependent coefficient is bounded using the explicit stability cap. The resulting constant depends only on curvature and friction. Taking one larger constant dominating all three coefficients makes its independence from particle count, dimension, and requested accuracy explicit.

steps.title: Termwise comparison with the supplied particle bound
steps.body:
For \(N\ge1\), \(D\le\sqrt N D+hN\sqrt{d_z}\) and \(\sqrt{d_z/N}\le\sqrt{Nd_z}\). The equilibrium term satisfies \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}=(1/\sqrt m)\sqrt{d_\theta/N}\). Apply the exponential rate bound, dominate each coefficient by \(C\), and add the three inequalities. This proves the exact printed shape, including the harmless nonnegative extra transient contribution \(hN\sqrt{d_z}\), from the sharper estimate.

The sharper thermal estimate can be enlarged term by term into the printed particle bound. Every enlargement adds a nonnegative quantity or uses \(N\ge1\). This derives the coarser displayed statement without asserting that its particle dependence is optimal.

steps.title: The bound for the particle parameter law
steps.body:
The final theorem starts from the unconditional KIPLMC2 RMS estimate and supplies every scalar hypothesis using the original curvature, friction and step restrictions. With \(D=W_2(\nu,\pi_N)\), it proves

\[\sqrt{\mathbb E\lVert\theta_n-\theta_\star\rVert^2}\le C\left[(\sqrt ND+hN\sqrt{d_z})e^{-mhn/(6\gamma)}+h\sqrt{Nd_z}+\sqrt{d_\theta/N}\right].\]

This is the supplied manuscript theorem with an explicit constant and the independent Gaussian algorithm law. The proof does not assume its desired RMS estimate as an input.

The scalar comparison is applied to the unconditional parameter theorem, with its initial transport discrepancy. Thus the coarser rate still describes the independent-Gaussian sampler. Its explicit constant makes clear which parameters are suppressed in asymptotic notation.

KIPLMC/KineticClock.lean.title: The physical-time integral equation under velocity and time scaling
KIPLMC/KineticClock.lean.summary:
Let \(Y_s\) solve the unit-temperature kinetic equation with sum force \(g\) and friction \(c\gamma\). The physical process is \(S_t=D_{c^{-1}}Y_{t/c}\), where \(D_a(v,x)=(av,x)\). This section proves the complete transformed integral equation in any complete normed vector space, including the L² space of random variables used by the Brownian construction.

The time and velocity change is performed inside the integral equation using bounded linearity and substitution. This gives a physical-flow identity compatible with the already proved Brownian scaling.

steps.title: Make velocity scaling a bounded linear map
steps.body:
The velocity projection multiplied by \(c\), paired with the unchanged position projection, defines a continuous linear map. Its action is exactly the velocity rescaling. Linearity allows this map to pass through Bochner integrals; continuity ensures the transformed path remains continuous. Expanding the phase drift proves \(c^{-1}D_{c^{-1}}R_{g,c\gamma}(z)=R_{c^{-2}g,\gamma}(D_{c^{-1}}z)\). The two powers of \(c^{-1}\) in the force come from time and velocity separately.

Velocity scaling is a bounded linear map on the full phase space. It therefore commutes with Bochner integration and preserves continuity of the constructed paths. Its position component is the identity, so physical parameter observables are unaffected.

steps.title: Change variables inside the integral equation
steps.body:
For \(0\le t\le T\), positivity of \(c\) gives \(t/c\in[0,T/c]\). Apply the continuous linear map to the given solution identity at \(t/c\), pass it through the integral, and substitute \(r=s/c\). The drift identity identifies the transformed force and friction, and the additive source becomes \(c^{-1}B_{t/c}\). One proves equality of the complete vector-valued integrals, not merely equality of differential expressions. This theorem requires no derivative of the Brownian input.

Apply the map to the original solution equation and perform the positive time substitution inside its drift integral. The force, friction, and thermal input transform with their stated factors. This proves an identity between integral solutions, not merely between formal differential equations.

KIPLMC/Continuous.lean.title: Brownian particle dynamics, Gibbs invariance, and convergence of position laws
KIPLMC/Continuous.lean.summary:
This section connects the specified Brownian kinetic diffusion to the physical particle system and proves Proposition 3 for its output law. The initial position is an arbitrary probability law with finite second moment. Standard Gaussian velocity and the specified Brownian source are independent of that position; velocity scaling gives the required physical thermal law. The Gibbs law is a proved stationary target, and the Wasserstein distance is the infimum over all couplings.

The constructed physical KIPLD process has the intended force, thermal initialization, and stationary target. Its law-level contraction and parameter projection separate dynamical mixing from finite-particle statistical error.

steps.title: The source, the physical flow, and its endpoint law
steps.body:
Set \(c=\sqrt N\). The specified probability source contains a standard Gaussian velocity and an independent vector Brownian source on the coordinate set \(\mathrm{Fin}(d_\theta)\sqcup(\mathrm{Fin}(N)\times\mathrm{Fin}(d_x))\). Use the proved selected kinetic flow with sum potential \(V_N\), smoothness \(NL\), and friction \(c\gamma\). The physical process is \(D_{c^{-1}}Y_{t/c}\). Position is unchanged, so its endpoint pushforward is exactly the constructed position law at time \(T/c\). This equality identifies the output measure in the convergence bound.

The source combines the prescribed position initialization, independent thermal Gaussian velocity, and specified Brownian process. The selected physical-time solution is a measurable function of these inputs. Projecting its endpoint defines the continuous particle position law.

steps.title: Verify the independent thermal initialization
steps.body:
The complete source law theorem supplies the initial phase law \(\mathcal N(0,I)\otimes\nu\). Push it through velocity multiplication by \(N^{-1/2}\). The result is precisely the independent thermal-velocity and position law; the velocity and position remain independent. The selected flow’s time-zero identity and the almost-everywhere scalar-multiplication rule identify the L² representatives with this pushforward. No initialization-law hypothesis is imposed on the final theorem.

The thermal initialization is the explicit inverse-square-root-particle Gaussian pushforward. Its independence from position and the entire Brownian source is proved by the product construction. This is precisely the phase/source law needed to transfer stationarity.

steps.title: Cancel the clock factors and prove stationary mixing
steps.body:
The lifted potential has curvature \(Nm\) and smoothness \(NL\). Multiplication by \(N\) transforms \(m+L\le\gamma^2\) into \(Nm+NL\le(\sqrt N\gamma)^2\), so the normalized Gibbs mixing theorem applies. Its exponent is \(-(Nm)/(\sqrt N\gamma)\,(T/\sqrt N)=-mT/\gamma\). The resulting estimate is \(W_2(\nu_T,\pi_Z)\le\sqrt2e^{-mT/\gamma}W_2(\nu,\pi_Z)\). The constructed theorem proves Gibbs stationarity internally. Separate moment and probability theorems prove that all real Wasserstein quantities are finite.

The clock transform turns the process into the shared unit-temperature diffusion for the sum potential. Curvature and friction scaling cancel in the physical-time mixing exponent. Since the target position is unchanged, the resulting convergence bound is directly a particle position estimate.

steps.title: The physical force in the integral equation
steps.body:
The drift lifted to L² represents pointwise application of the true sum gradient. The almost-everywhere scalar multiplication and composition identities show that \(N^{-1}\mathcal G(\nabla V_N)=\mathcal G(F)\), where \(F=\nabla V_N/N\) is the previously verified particle force. Apply the exact kinetic clock theorem to the selected constructed solution. The result is the full physical-time integral equation with friction \(\gamma\), the force \(F\), and input \(N^{-1/2}B_{t/\sqrt N}\). The shared Brownian scaling theorem identifies its thermal amplitude as \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\).

The average-potential gradient identity rewrites the transformed drift as the parameter-average and latent-pair force. Consequently the constructed physical path solves the intended KIPLD equation. This identification links the law-level mixing theorem to the stated particle dynamics.

steps.title: Project to the parameter and add the statistical error
steps.body:
The parameter projection has operator norm at most one, so pushing any coupling through it cannot increase its quadratic cost. Taking the infimum over initial couplings bounds the parameter Wasserstein distance by the full position distance. The initial independent coupling \(\nu\otimes\pi_Z\) bounds that infimum by \((\mathbb E\|Z_0-\bar Z_*\|^2)^{1/2}\), giving precisely the printed proposition. A second estimate adds the already proved sharp equilibrium concentration radius \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\) by the L² triangle inequality, giving a direct parameter RMS bound about the unique marginal-likelihood maximizer.

Nonexpansive parameter projection transfers the sampling transport error. The powered Gibbs marginal contributes the sharp statistical radius around the likelihood maximizer. Their sum yields a continuous-time parameter RMS bound with separate dynamical and finite-particle contributions.

KIPLMC/Accuracy.lean.title: Particle count, step length, and iteration count for a prescribed error
KIPLMC/Accuracy.lean.summary:
These corollaries turn both particle-sampler theorems into finite epsilon guarantees. Statistical concentration, discretization, and initialization receive separate error bounds. Integer ceilings and positive minimum steps make the prescriptions valid without informal asymptotic rounding.

Particle count, step size, and iteration count control separate statistical, numerical, and transient errors. Positive minimum steps and natural-number ceilings turn the two sampler bounds into finite accuracy prescriptions.

steps.title: Control KIPLMC1 with three explicit error bounds
steps.body:
Write its bound as \(\sqrt2(1-\alpha)^nD+b+s\). Allocate \(b,s\le\varepsilon/3\), and choose the logarithmic count so the geometric factor times \(D\) is at most \(\varepsilon/24\). These fit within the shared \(0.94\varepsilon\) persistent-error allocation. The algorithm theorem supplies the bound internally, with its Gaussian law and MMLE target. Only choices of \(N,h,n\) remain in the hypotheses. Since \(b=(\sqrt2 L/m)h\sqrt{d_\theta/N+d_x}\) and \(s=\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), the formula exposes the first method’s dimension and accuracy dependence directly.

The statistical and discretization errors each receive an explicit fraction of the requested error. The remaining geometric transient is reduced by the rounded logarithmic iteration count. The sum of these verified allocations proves the requested parameter accuracy for the first sampler.

steps.title: Round the exponential and statistical requirements
steps.body:
The exponential error bound uses \(n\ge\lceil\max\{0,\log(24D/\varepsilon)/\alpha\}\rceil\), with a separate zero-\(D\) case. Monotonicity of the exponential and \(e^{-\log x}=x^{-1}\) give \(De^{-\alpha n}\le\varepsilon/24\). For a square-root statistical term \(C\sqrt{d/N}\), choose \(N=\max\{1,\lceil9C^2d/\varepsilon^2\rceil\}\). The ceiling inequality, multiplication through \(N>0\), and the square-root identity prove the statistical term is at most \(\varepsilon/3\). Zero parameter dimension is included.

The particle ceiling ensures a positive integer count and the desired concentration-error bound, including zero parameter dimension. The iteration ceiling similarly converts a real decay threshold into a valid integer iteration count. The zero-initial-error case avoids taking an unnecessary positive logarithm.

steps.title: Choose the step and inspect the dimension algebra
steps.body:
For a positive stability cap \(A\) and positive linear-bias coefficient \(B\), the explicit choice \(h=\min\{A,\varepsilon/(3B)\}\) is positive, respects stability, and has \(hB\le\varepsilon/3\). This applies to each method’s displayed bias. The exact source identity \(\sqrt{N(d_\theta+Nd_x)}=(d_\theta/\varepsilon)\sqrt{1+d_x/\varepsilon^2}\) at the idealized choice \(N=d_\theta/\varepsilon^2\) explains the supplied KIPLMC2 complexity. Integer ceilings affect constants and are handled by the previous theorem. One proves the identity by equality of nonnegative squares.

The minimum step enforces stability and a linear discretization-error bound simultaneously. Substituting the particle prescription into the dimension factor explains the source’s small-error scaling. Integer rounding is controlled separately rather than hidden inside the idealized algebra.

steps.title: Apply the supplied KIPLMC2 rate with its uniform constant
steps.body:
Let \(C\) be the explicit constant depending only on curvature and friction, and set \(A=\sqrt N D_0+hN\sqrt{d_z}\). Apply the rounded exponential error bound to \(D=CA\), with \(\alpha=mh/(6\gamma)\). Allocate \(Ch\sqrt{Nd_z}\le\varepsilon/3\) and \(C\sqrt{d_\theta/N}\le\varepsilon/3\). The Gaussian-chain theorem then gives RMS error at most \(\varepsilon\). For fixed curvature constants, the particle choice has order \(d_\theta/\varepsilon^2\), the small-error step has order \(\varepsilon^3/(d_\theta\sqrt{d_x})\), and the displayed reciprocal-step logarithmic threshold yields the source’s iteration order. Polynomial growth of initial distance is the additional condition under which that logarithm is suppressed in the source’s tilde notation.

The second method’s printed bound has both a persistent particle-dependent bias and an additional transient coefficient. Both enter the rounded prescription. Suppressing the initialization logarithm in asymptotic notation requires the stated growth condition on the initial discrepancy.

KIPLMC/Stationarity.lean.title: Gibbs invariance of the physical-time particle phase law
KIPLMC/Stationarity.lean.summary:
The invariant density calculation is proved as an identity of phase laws: the complete physical Brownian phase process, started at its normalized Gaussian-times-Gibbs target, has that same target distribution at every nonnegative time.

The exact clock conjugacy transfers the full unit-temperature stationary phase law to the physical particle temperature. Position is unchanged, so the stationary parameter marginal remains the powered likelihood.

steps.title: Transport the proved full phase stationarity through the exact clock
steps.body:
The constructed selected flow for the sum potential preserves \(\mathcal N(0,I)\otimes\pi_Z\), by the shared kinetic stationarity theorem. Push this endpoint law through \(D_{1/\sqrt N}(v,z)=(v/\sqrt N,z)\). The product pushforward is exactly \(\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\otimes\pi_Z\), namely the kinetic Gibbs target. The physical KIPLD flow was defined by this very time and velocity change. The almost-everywhere identity for scalar multiplication identifies its L² phase representative with the pushed constructed representative. This proves invariance of the whole phase law, including velocity–position independence, rather than only the position marginal or a formal zero-generator calculation.

The unit-temperature kinetic flow has the full Gaussian-times-Gibbs stationary phase law. The proved clock-and-velocity conjugacy transports that law to thermal covariance \(I/N\) and the same position Gibbs marginal. Hence the physical KIPLD integral solution is stationary under its phase target.

KIPLMC/LogisticExample.lean.title: Logistic regression derivatives, convexity, and failure of uniform strong convexity
KIPLMC/LogisticExample.lean.summary:
The Bayesian logistic example has a Gaussian location prior and finitely many Bernoulli observations. The model is \(U(\theta,x)=\frac{\tau}{2}\|x-\theta\|^2+\sum_j[\log(1+e^{\langle v_j,x\rangle})-y_j\langle v_j,x\rangle]\), where \(\tau=\sigma^{-2}\). Additive normalization constants do not affect any derivative. This chapter derives the joint gradient and its Fréchet derivative, proves the exact global smoothness constant printed in the paper, and proves convexity and the full-span strict-convexity statement. It also proves that no finite unregularized model in a nonzero latent dimension has a positive global strong-convexity constant. Consequently the experimental model illustrates the algorithms but does not automatically satisfy the hypotheses of the quantitative convergence theorems.

The full joint derivatives distinguish global smoothness, pointwise strict convexity, and uniform strong convexity. Common-translation directions prove that finite unregularized logistic models need additional regularization for the global quantitative convergence assumptions.

steps.title: Differentiate a single observation
steps.body:
For a single response, write \(\ell_y(u)=\log(1+e^u)-yu\). The logarithm is evaluated at a positive argument, so the ordinary chain rule gives \(\ell_y'(u)=e^u/(1+e^u)-y=s(u)-y\). First, the argument identifies the sigmoid with this exponential ratio, then composes the exponential and logarithm derivative rules. The curvature is \(q(u)=s(u)(1-s(u))\). Since \(0<s(u)<1\), it is positive. The identity \(q(u)=1/4-(s(u)-1/2)^2\) gives \(q(u)\le1/4\). The mean-value theorem therefore supplies a global \(1/4\)-Lipschitz theorem for the sigmoid. These arguments do not require the response to be binary; the source's Bernoulli choices are included.

The response label enters the first derivative but cancels from the second derivative. Logistic curvature therefore depends only on the predictor. Its pointwise positivity and global upper bound distinguish strict convexity along observed directions from a uniform lower curvature bound.

steps.title: The first and second variations from the model
steps.body:
Take any affine joint line \((\theta,x)+t(u,w)\). The prior contributes \(\tau\langle x-\theta+t(w-u),w-u\rangle\) to the score. Observation \(j\) contributes \([s(\langle v_j,x+tw\rangle)-y_j]\langle v_j,w\rangle\). Differentiating this scalar function again gives \(\tau\|w-u\|^2+\sum_jq(\langle v_j,x+tw\rangle)\langle v_j,w\rangle^2\). The proof constructs the derivative of each affine coordinate, applies the squared-norm rule and the single-observation rule, and adds the finitely many derivatives. The second proof differentiates the resulting score. Thus the displayed quadratic form is justified by calculus on the original potential.

The common-translation direction \(u=w\) removes the Gaussian prior contribution entirely. Curvature in that direction must come from observations. The displayed second variation therefore reveals both the prior’s nullspace and the role of feature span in identifying the full joint state.

steps.title: Find the exact Hessian nullspace
steps.body:
Every term in the second variation is nonnegative when \(\tau\ge0\). If \(\tau>0\), a zero total forces \(w-u=0\) and \(\langle v_j,w\rangle=0\) for every feature. Conversely those equations make every term vanish. The proof isolates the nonnegative prior term, bounds each observation term by the whole sum, and uses strict positivity of every logistic weight to cancel it. If the features span the latent space, orthogonality to every feature extends to their linear span by submodule induction. Taking the inner product with \(w\) itself then gives \(w=0\), and hence \(u=0\). Every nonzero joint direction therefore has strictly positive second variation at each finite state.

Because every finite predictor has a positive logistic weight, zero observation curvature means orthogonality to every feature. Full span eliminates that nullspace at each finite state. This is a pointwise positive-definiteness statement; it does not provide a positive lower eigenvalue uniformly over all states.

steps.title: Global convexity and full-span strict convexity
steps.body:
To compare two joint states \(z,z'\), restrict the potential to \(F(t)=U(z+t(z'-z))\). The two derivative theorems identify \(F''\) with the nonnegative quadratic form. The real-variable second-derivative criterion proves convexity of \(F\). Applying its Jensen inequality at \(t=0,1\) yields the full joint convexity inequality. Under the span assumption and \(z\ne z'\), the direction is nonzero, so the second derivative is positive at every finite \(t\). The strict second-derivative criterion yields strict Jensen inequality. The argument explicitly rewrites \(z+b(z'-z)=az+bz'\) using \(a+b=1\), so the conclusion concerns the original joint potential on the whole space.

Convexity is proved on arbitrary line segments, so it is a global property of the joint potential. Strict positivity of the second derivative on each nonconstant segment yields strict convexity. The argument does not turn the varying second-derivative lower bound into a uniform constant.

steps.title: Use the Euclidean norm for the joint gradient
steps.body:
The source norm is the Euclidean product norm \(\|(\theta,x)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+\|x\|^2\). The joint state is equipped with this Euclidean Hilbert norm for the gradient claims. The coordinate equivalence is continuous and linear. Differentiating the prior and all finite observations proves Fréchet differentiability. The explicit gradient is \((-\tau(x-\theta),\;\tau(x-\theta)+\sum_j[s(\langle v_j,x\rangle)-y_j]v_j)\). To identify it with the Hilbert gradient, compare the Fréchet derivative on an arbitrary direction with the directional derivative above. Expanding the product inner product gives the same functional, so uniqueness of derivatives proves the gradient formula. The resulting equality is with the gradient, not a separately named surrogate force.

The Euclidean joint norm is needed because the gradient is defined through its inner product with arbitrary joint directions. A maximum product norm would not give that Hilbert gradient interpretation. The explicit formula therefore uses the same geometry as the smoothness and Hessian statements.

steps.title: The exact printed global smoothness constant
steps.body:
The prior block maps a joint difference \((a,b)\) to \((a-b,b-a)\). Its squared norm is \(2\|b-a\|^2\le4(\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2)\), hence its operator norm is at most two. For observation \(j\), the sigmoid Lipschitz bound and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(\|(s(\langle v_j,x\rangle)-s(\langle v_j,x'\rangle))v_j\|\le\frac14\|v_j\|^2\|x-x'\|\). The latent coordinate projection has norm at most one. Adding these bounds proves \(\|\nabla U(z)-\nabla U(z')\|\le(2\tau+\frac14\sum_j\|v_j\|^2)\|z-z'\|\). The proof first proves the squared-norm estimate, then bounds each summand, and finally decomposes the gradient difference into its prior and observation parts. With \(\tau=\sigma^{-2}\), this is exactly the source constant.

The prior couples parameter and latent directions through a block operator with norm two. Each observation contributes a rank-one latent operator with norm bounded by one quarter of its squared feature norm. Summing these operator bounds yields the printed global Lipschitz constant.

steps.title: The full block Hessian as a Fréchet derivative
steps.body:
The operator is \(\nabla^2U(\theta,x)=\tau\begin{pmatrix}I&-I\\-I&I\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&\sum_jq(\langle v_j,x\rangle)v_jv_j^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}\). Each rank-one observation block sends a direction \((u,w)\) to \((0,q_j\langle v_j,w\rangle v_j)\). The argument constructs these maps as continuous linear maps, forms their finite sum, and transports the block operator to the Euclidean joint space. Differentiating both gradient coordinates with the Fréchet chain rule gives exactly this operator. Expanding its product inner product recovers the earlier curvature formula. Thus the block matrix printed in the example is the Fréchet derivative of the joint gradient.

The block Hessian is obtained by differentiating the joint gradient. Its quadratic form recovers exactly the previously derived line second variation. These equalities establish agreement between the coordinate formula, directional calculus, and the operator used in theoretical assumptions.

steps.title: An explicit full-rank counterexample separates strict from strong convexity
steps.body:
Already one scalar feature \(v_1=1\) spans the latent space. With response one and common location \(\theta=x=t\), the Gaussian prior vanishes and \(U(t,t)=\log(1+e^{-t})\). For \(t\ge0\), this lies between zero and \(\log2\). A positive strong-convexity constant \(m\) would force the midpoint inequality between \((0,0)\) and \((2t,2t)\) to contain the negative correction \(-mt^2\). Choosing \(t^2=(\log2+1)/m\) makes that right-hand side negative, contradicting nonnegativity. One proves the logarithm identity, both bounds, the exact Euclidean distance, and this contradiction. The full-span theorem applies to this example, so strict convexity is compatible with failure of every positive uniform lower curvature bound.

Along common positive translation in the one-feature example, the potential remains bounded while a strongly convex function would grow quadratically away from its midpoint. The contradiction is explicit despite full feature rank. Thus strict convexity alone cannot justify the sampler’s strong-convexity convergence theorem.

steps.title: The strong-convexity caveat for every finite unregularized model
steps.body:
The obstruction is general. For every real response and predictor, \(\ell_y(u)\le\log2+(1+|y|)|u|\), because \(1+e^u\le2e^{|u|}\). Along any nonzero common translation \((\theta,x)=(tw,tw)\), the prior stays zero, while the finitely many observation terms grow at most linearly: \(U(tw,tw)\le|J|\log2+|t|C_w\), where \(C_w=\sum_j(1+|y_j|)|\langle v_j,w\rangle|\). Applying a hypothetical strong-convexity midpoint inequality to the opposite states at \(\pm t\) forces \(m\|w\|^2t^2\le C_wt\). Choose \(t=(C_w+1)/(m\|w\|^2)>0\) to contradict it. This proves the source caveat in every nonzero latent dimension, regardless of feature rank. It explains why further regularization is needed before applying the paper's global strong-convexity convergence bounds to these experiments.

For any finite observation set, common translation eliminates the prior and leaves at most linear growth of the observation losses. Uniform strong convexity would require quadratic growth in that same nonzero direction. Additional regularization is therefore necessary to meet the global quantitative hypotheses in these unregularized examples.
